newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany wages multi-front battle to save dike.
newsitem.headline: Germany wages multi-front battle to save dike.

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers were struggling on several fronts on Saturday in what appeared to be a losing battle to shore up crumbling dikes on the Oder river threatening to unleash massive floods.

Soldiers and relief workers who spent the day battling to reinforce sodden flood barriers near the towns of Hohenwutzen and Reitwein faced another emergency when officials reported a weakening of the dike close to the village of Zollbruecke.

New cracks continue to appear in the line of dikes that hold back the river forming part of Germany's eastern border with Poland, keeping it from pouring into a low-lying 800 square km basin of fertile farmland.
The German army has staged a spectacular effort to save the dikes, deploying thousands of soldiers, dozens of helicopters and tonnes of sand and gravel to plug weak spots in the dike.
But after nearly two weeks of constant toil where whole villages have come out to help fill sandbags, it is becoming more likely that the river will prove too strong.
"We must have hope but the chances are not great," said Matthias Platzeck, environment minister of Brandenburg state.
"There is not a single point in the dike now where there isn't a problem," he added.
"The chances that the dike will break are more probable than that we will be able to hold it," said a spokesman for the flood crisis committee in nearby Bad Freienwalde.
Soldiers and aid workers were felling trees in the area to allow helicopters to fly in and drop sand to reinforce the dike.

"We can see that this permanent water pressure is slowly making the dike sodden along the whole stretch of the river," Platzeck said, adding that the situation at Zollbruecke was not yet as serious as at the other two crisis points.

The flood waters have already claimed more than 100 lives in Poland and the Czech Republic. They have threatened the entire Oderbruch basin for more than a week, weakening the dikes to the point of collapse.

The looming failure of the most fragile dike at Hohenwutzen threatened to flood an area 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long on Germany's border with Poland, submerging dozens of villages, farms and factories.
The last time a break in the dike flooded the Oderbruch region was in 1947 near Reitwein. Before that there was a break near Zollbruecke in 1838.
The region is vulnerable because it lies below the river, which presses against the twists and turns in the dike as the Oder runs north and empties into the Baltic Sea.

The Oderbruch basin was created 250 years ago by Frederik the Great of Prussia, who drained the swamps and redirected the route of the Oder, gaining a huge valley of arable land as part of Prussia's eastward expansion.
But now weeks of flooding and relentless rainstorms seem to be driving the river to seek its original banks, which are now covered with fields of grains, golden sunflowers and sugar beet.

Around 15,000 people have been evacuated from the region since last week and thousands more were warned to be ready to leave their homes at a moment's notice as the likelihood of a dam break grows daily.
"We won't be able to stop holding our breath until the water level drops at least one and a half metres (five feet)," said Platzeck.
